## 3. Module boundaries

```
cairn/
  packages/
    core/          pure domain. zero runtime deps. no DOM, no fetch, no fs,
                   no Date.now() and no randomness in logic (injected clock + IdFactory).
    client/        trip store, ports, selectors. Platform-agnostic: no DOM, no React,
                   no network in Phase 1. Runs and is tested in plain Node.
    tokens/        colors, category labels, mode icons. No logic.
  apps/
    web/           Vite + React. Port implementations + views. Installable.
    mobile/        Expo SDK 56. The ONLY place expo-location / expo-media-library may be imported.
  services/
    api/           Node 24 + Postgres/RLS. Auth, trips, social graph, permissions, ticket storage.
    ingest/        Mailbox polling + parsing. Writes IngestCandidate rows and nothing else.
                   Separate deploy unit, separate credentials, no write grant on trip tables.
  db/              SQL migrations + RLS policies + the policy conformance test
  fixtures/        europe2026.sha256, europe2026.bookings.json, golden/
  tools/           extract-legacy.mjs and other one-shot scripts
  docs/            BRIEF, ARCHITECTURE, ROADMAP, BUILD-NOTES, QA-FINDINGS, REVIEW
```

Dependency direction, enforced by **a test that walks imports and does not currently exist** — write it;
four packages is when it is cheap, and the property holds today so it is a guard, not a repair. `core` →
nothing. `tokens` → nothing. `client` → core. `web`/`mobile` → client, core, tokens. `api`/`ingest` → core.
**Nothing imports `web` or `mobile`.** This is the boundary that rots first.

The same test carries one more assertion, which is a privacy boundary rather than a tidiness one:
**nothing under `apps/` may import `tools/extract-legacy.mjs`, directly or transitively.** `apps/web` reads
trip data only from the generated, redacted sample file (§6.6). That is what keeps the live planner's
credentials out of a bundle by construction rather than by remembering.

`services/ingest` having no write grant on trip tables is a security boundary, not tidiness: the component
holding mailbox credentials must not be able to modify an itinerary.

---

## 4. The Phase 1 client — local-first, multi-trip

Jacob's answer widened Phase 1: the engine **plus a working multi-trip UI he can open and use**. No server,
no accounts. This section specifies it tightly enough that the builder does not invent it.

**Which client: web first.** Vite + React + TypeScript. It is the surface Jacob, the builder, the tester and
a friend with a link can all run today with no device, no store review and no account — and per §1.3, desktop
planning is where this half of the product belongs permanently anyway.

### 4.1 Shape

```
packages/client/src/
  store/      TripStore — a reducer over core's build functions, plus history and persistence bookkeeping
  ports/      StoragePort, FilePort, MapPort, ClockPort, IdPort   (SyncPort arrives in Phase 2)
  selectors/  thin memoised wrappers over core's derive functions
apps/web/src/
  ports/      IndexedDB storage · download + <input type=file> · Leaflet map
  views/      React components. No domain logic. No core mutation outside dispatch.
```

### 4.2 State model

```ts
type AppState = {
  library: TripSummaryRow[];   // the shipped shape is {id,title,startDate,endDate,cityCount,dayCount,
                               // stopCount,poolCount,revision} — cheap, always loaded. (Revisions 1–8 said
                               // `updatedAt`, which has never existed; corrected in revision 9, and §8.4
                               // widens the row and states the freshness rule that keeps it honest.)
  activeTripId: TripId | null;
  doc: Trip | null;            // exactly ONE trip in memory at a time
  derived: DerivedCache;       // legs, roll-ups, clusters, conflicts, issues — keyed by (doc identity, today)
  ui: UiState;                 // activeDay, activeCity, mapScope, selection, panels — NEVER in the doc
  history: { past: Trip[]; future: Trip[]; limit: 50 };
  persistence: {
    savedDoc: Trip | null;                 // the document storage last agreed with us about — §2.2b F2.
                                           // Answers "is there an unwritten edit" AND is the merge ancestor.
    savedVersion: StorageVersion | null;   // the WRITE FENCE — §2.2a. `null` = nothing stored yet.
    status: 'idle'|'saving'|'error'|'conflict'; lastError?: string;
  };
};
```

**`savedRevision` is deleted** (revision 4, QA R4-1). It had one remaining consumer, `dirty()`, and that
consumer was the bug; a field left in place is a field the next person compares. `savedDoc` replaces it and
also absorbs the store's module-level `baseDoc`, so there is exactly one pointer to "what storage last agreed
with us about" instead of two facts that can disagree. Because it lives in `persistence` it moves only inside
a `set()`, so no subscriber can render an indicator computed against a pointer the state it was handed does
not contain.

**`savedVersion` and `savedDoc` are assigned from a port result and from nowhere else** — `load()`'s
`{doc, version}`, or a successful `saveIfVersion()` (paired with the document that write carried). Neither is
ever computed from the in-memory document, and **neither is touched by the reducer**, including by
`undo`/`redo`: undo changes the document, not what storage holds. That one sentence is what makes R3-1
structurally unreachable, and it is why `savedDoc` is safe where `savedRevision` was not — it is a *pointer
to bytes that were written*, not a number the document owns.

Six rules, each of which exists because of a specific failure:

1. **Every mutation is `dispatch(action)`, and every action maps 1:1 onto a core build function.** The
   reducer holds no domain logic — it is `doc = core[action.fn](doc, ...args)` plus history and persistence
   bookkeeping. If a feature needs logic the reducer cannot express, the logic goes into core. This is the
   mechanism that keeps web and native from drifting: it is `CLAUDE.md`'s "one data structure drives every
   view", one level up.
2. **`ui` is never persisted into the trip document.** Today the app stores drag order in localStorage keyed
   by `CONTENT_VERSION`, and that conflation is exactly why the cache went stale for a week. Stop order is
   *document* data (`placement.order`); which day is open is *UI* state.
3. **Derived data is never stored, and is invalidated wholesale on `(document identity, today)`.** No partial
   invalidation — cheap at 112 stops, and it removes a class of stale-view bugs outright. Revision 4: the key
   was `(revision, tripId)` and `===` on a revision cannot prove sameness (§2.2a rule 1), so undo-then-a-
   different-edit served the pre-undo document's legs and conflicts — and, through `syncResolutions`, *wrote*
   from them. §2.2b F2. The same defect exists in any view-level memo keyed on `derived.revision`
   (`DayMap`'s effect dependency array is one) and is fixed the same way: depend on the cache object, not on
   a number inside it.
4. **Autosave** writes the whole document, debounced 400 ms. `state.doc !== persistence.savedDoc` drives the
   dirty indicator (§2.2b F2).
   A failed write puts `persistence.status = 'error'` and says so on screen; it never fails silently.
   **The write is compare-and-set, and the compare happens inside the port.** `StoragePort` exposes
   `saveIfVersion(id, expectedVersion, doc, summary)` and nothing else that writes: the comparison and
   the write are one indivisible step (one IndexedDB `readwrite` transaction; one synchronous block in the
   in-memory port). The expectation is `persistence.savedVersion` — the opaque storage token of §2.2a, **not
   `doc.revision`**. If the stored version has moved, the write is refused, `status` becomes `'conflict'`,
   and the indicator says so. **A tab whose write was refused MUST NOT display "Saved."**

   It is worth being explicit about why the compare cannot live in the store, because the first fix put it
   there and it did not hold. `load()` → compare → `save()` is two awaits with an interleaving point in
   the middle: two tabs both read revision *R*, both passed the compare, and the second write destroyed
   the first while **both** displayed "Saved" (QA R2-1, two runs in three). No amount of checking above
   the port closes that window. Two tabs on one trip is not an exotic case; it is Jacob with a second
   window open.

   The store also serializes its **own** saves, chaining each attempt onto the last, so an autosave and an
   explicit `flush()` cannot overlap. A tab that conflicts with itself has no other writer to merge with,
   which makes it an unresolvable state rather than a recoverable one.

   **4a. A write the store declines to install may not move the fence** (revision 8, QA R11-1; the ruling,
   its alternatives and its reasoning are **§2.2a A-7**, and this rule is not implementable without it).

   > `persistence.savedDoc` and `persistence.savedVersion` advance **together**, and only to a document this
   > store still holds or may legitimately write forward over: at the moment the write settles, either
   > `state.doc === startedFrom` or `toWrite === startedFrom`. A successful write whose document the store
   > declines to install advances neither field, installs nothing, re-arms no debounce, and leaves
   > `status: 'conflict'` with the user's edit in `doc` and the indicator not reading "Saved".

   Rule 4 already says `savedVersion`/`savedDoc` come from a port result and nowhere else. That was
   necessary and not sufficient: the port result is a fact about **the bytes that were written**, and
   `writeAndSettle` was recording it as a fact about **the document the store holds**. When a merge writes a
   document the user has since typed past, those are different documents, the store keeps a fence it has no
   right to, and the next ordinary autosave writes an un-merged document over another writer's work with the
   fence's blessing and the chip on *Saved* — §0.6 reached one level out from where §2.2a found it. The two
   autosave call sites satisfy the second disjunct by construction and do not change; the merged write is
   the only site in the system where `toWrite !== startedFrom`.

5. **Undo/redo is snapshot-based** over the immutable `Trip`, limit 50. Structural sharing makes this cheap.
   The restored snapshot is byte-identical to the document it captured, `revision` included; it carries no
   authority over `savedVersion` (rule 4, §2.2a).

   **One carve-out, and it is exactly one field (revision 6, QA R8-1).** `resolutions[].retiredAt` is
   monotone metadata, not history: §2.7's A-5 ledger re-asserts it onto every restored snapshot, inside the
   same `set()`, before any subscriber sees the state. So the guarantee reads, precisely: *the restored
   snapshot is byte-identical to the document it captured except that a `resolutions[]` row whose `retiredAt`
   was `null` may be restored carrying the date the ledger already holds for its `conflictId`, and `revision`
   is bumped when that happens.* Nothing else moves — not a day, not a stop, not a place, not a booking, not
   a resolution's `state`, `by`, `at` or `note`, and not a row the ledger has no key for. `reassertRetirements`
   is a pure function whose only writable field is `retiredAt`, so this is enforced by the function's shape
   and not by discipline, and the test asserts field-by-field equality over everything else.

   The reducer's `undo`/`redo` stay pure snapshot restores and gain nothing: the ledger is applied by the
   store, above them. **Retirement still never consumes an undo slot and is still never a user edit** — it
   does not push onto `history.past`, and pressing undo *N* times reverts *N* of the user's own edits.
6. **A pending write is never outlived by its document.** The five NO-SILENT-LOSS cases the criterion
   enumerated all keep the edit in memory; QA R3-2 found the sixth, where the edit's *container* goes away —
   a 400 ms debounced write is still pending and the active document is replaced, closed or deleted, so the
   timer fires against a document that is no longer there and the edit is gone with nothing on screen. One
   click, no second tab, inside a window the app chose. Three rules close it:

   **6a. Every transition that changes the active document flushes first.** `closeTrip`, `openTrip`,
   `createTrip`, `adoptTrip`, `importDoc`, `deleteTrip` — that is the complete list, and it is a **closed
   list**: a seventh path that assigns `state.doc` is a defect. Each begins with `await flush()`, which
   cancels the pending timer and awaits the write.

   **6a′ (revision 4, QA R4-1). The flush may be skipped only on the F2 predicate.** `flushForTransition`
   is allowed to avoid rewriting a 176 KB document on every navigation, and that optimisation is where the
   whole of rule 6 was lost: it asked `doc.revision !== savedRevision`, a *content counter*, whether an edit
   would be lost — and undo makes that counter non-injective over content, so a fresh, different edit landing
   on a revision number an earlier edit already used made the store report "nothing to write", skip the
   write, complete the switch, and display "Saved" over a document storage did not hold. One click, no
   second tab, nothing on screen — R3-2's symptom sentence reached through the predicate rather than through
   the timer. The skip now requires **all three** of `status === 'idle'`, no pending debounce timer, and
   `state.doc === state.persistence.savedDoc`; the third is the real condition and the other two can only
   ever cause more writing. `flush()` stays unconditional and must never consult the predicate.

   **6a″ (revision 3, QA R5-1; the bound blessed and its exits ruled in revision 5, QA R6-1/R6-2). The flush
   is a loop, bounded by `FLUSH_MAX_ATTEMPTS = 5`.** A flush is not a moment — it is an `await` long enough
   for the user to type into — so the exit condition is `dirty()`, re-asserted *after* every write and never
   sampled before one. The loop needs a bound because a user typing through every write could otherwise hold
   a transition open forever, and a hang is not an improvement on data loss.

   **Five is right, and the reason is that the bound is not a timeout.** Each pass awaits its own write, so
   slow storage makes the loop *take longer*, it does not make it exhaust; the bound is only reached by a
   document that will not settle. Convergence in the realistic worst case takes two passes — the in-flight
   document, then the one that arrived behind it — and a transition is a *click*, not a typing session, so a
   third pass already means something unusual is happening. Five is two plus three of headroom, and it does
   not need to grow with document size, device speed or trip length. If a future phase finds it exhausted in
   the field, that is a defect report about what will not settle, not a reason to raise the number.

   **Exhausting the bound is a refusal, for display as well as for control flow.** It was the one path that
   aborted a transition without telling anyone: `flushForTransition` returned `false`, the caller returned
   `state` unchanged, `status` was still `'idle'`, and no banner reads `'idle'` — so the click did nothing
   and said nothing. Rule 6b's sentence is *"aborts the transition **and tells the user**"*, and this exit
   owes the same debt as the other two. Concretely, the give-up path sets `persistence.status = 'error'` with
   a `lastError` that names what happened — *"Couldn't finish saving before switching. Your edit is still
   here."* — so the **existing** error banner renders, offering the two recoveries it already offers (retry,
   export this copy). Not `'conflict'`: nothing refused the write and there is no other writer to merge with,
   so offering a merge would be a lie about what went wrong. No new UI mechanism; §4.2 rule 6b's refusal path
   already reaches the screen this way and this exit joins it.

   **And the debounce is re-armed when the loop gives up while the document is dirty.** The loop cancels the
   pending timer on every pass (`cancelTimer()`), including the pass on which it gives up — so before this
   ruling the store was left dirty, `'idle'`, and with **no scheduled write at all** until the user's next
   keystroke. Cancelling work the user's own edit had scheduled and not putting it back is a bug on its own
   terms, independent of the banner. So: on the bound-exhausted exit, if `dirty()`, re-arm the ordinary
   debounce.

   Re-arming automatically is the right shape, and the alternatives are worse for stated reasons. A
   "Retry" button alone leaves a dirty document with nothing scheduled, which is the defect. A dedicated
   retry loop with backoff is a second scheduler on the write path, and §4.2 has one. What is re-armed is the
   **ordinary** debounced `attemptSave`, not another `flushForTransition`, so it cannot recurse into the loop;
   if that write also leaves the document dirty it re-arms only through the normal `scheduleSave` path, which
   is what typing does anyway. When it lands, `status` returns to `'idle'` and the banner clears — the message
   is honestly transient. **The transition is never retried automatically**: the user clicks again. An app
   that navigates by itself some seconds after a click the user has already given up on is worse than one
   that does nothing.

   **The other two exits do not re-arm, and this is a three-way rule the builder must not flatten.** On
   `'conflict'`, a re-armed autosave would spin against a fence that will refuse it every 400 ms; the user
   must merge or export. On `'error'`, the port is failing and the banner's Retry is the deliberate act. Only
   the bound-exhausted exit re-arms, because it is the only one where nothing has actually refused anything.
   In all three, `isDirty()` stays true, the indicator does not read "Saved", and the edit is still in `doc`.

   **6b. If the flush cannot succeed, the transition does not happen.** A refusal (`'conflict'`) or a storage
   failure (`'error'`) aborts the switch: the old document stays active, still holds the edit, the indicator
   does not read "Saved", and the screen names the two things the user can actually do — merge with the
   stored copy, or export this copy. *Discarding the edit with a notice would satisfy the letter of "the app
   says so" and violate the product: this is a local-first, single-owner app whose stated conventions are
   that the user's content is authoritative and that conflicts are surfaced rather than resolved by guessing.
   Blocking is only tolerable because it is rare — it fires when a write genuinely cannot land, not on every
   navigation, which is why "flush" and not "prompt" is the default path.*

   **6c. `deleteTrip` of the active trip is the one exception, and it is explicit.** The pending timer is
   cancelled *without* writing and the transition proceeds — the user asked for that document to be
   destroyed, and 6b would otherwise make a conflicted trip undeletable. The delete confirmation names the
   trip.

   **The exception is about not *writing*. It is not about not *ordering*** (revision 5, QA R7-3). The
   parenthetical this rule used to end on — *"a stray timer surviving a delete would be harmless anyway: its
   expectation matches no record"* — was wrong, and wrong in the direction that costs data. A write already
   queued on the store's serialization chain can settle *after* `ports.storage.delete(id)` returns; an
   expect-absent write (`expectedVersion: null`) is then **satisfied** by the record's absence, so it
   succeeds, `upsertSummary` puts the library row back, and the trip is resurrected with the delete silently
   undone. QA measured it: `in storage=true in library=true`. It is not reachable through the shipped UI
   today, and that is luck, not design.

   So: **`delete()` goes on the serialization chain, as a link of its own** — §4.3. `deleteTrip` does not
   merely `await saving` and then call the port. `await saving; ports.storage.delete(id)` is a check-then-act
   with an interleaving point in the middle, which is §0.6's error one level up from where §2.2a found it:
   between the await resolving and the call, another link can be appended and land concurrently with the
   delete. Putting the delete *on* the chain gives the store one total order over every mutation it issues,
   which is the property `chainOntoSaving` already exists to provide. The link is *"drain, delete, forget"*
   and all three happen inside it: the port delete, the library row removal, and — when the deleted trip was
   the active one — the reset of `doc`, `savedDoc` and `savedVersion`, so that no later link can observe a
   half-deleted store or write against a fence pointer for a trip that no longer exists.

   None of that reopens the exception: the *active* trip's pending timer is still cancelled without writing,
   so the queue the delete link drains contains only writes the store had **already committed to** before the
   user asked for the deletion, and a conflicted trip is still deletable — a refused write ahead of the delete
   in the chain reports its own failure and the delete still runs behind it.

   Belt and braces, because a timer that fires late must not be able to hurt anything: **a scheduled save
   captures the trip id it was scheduled for**, and if `state.doc` is no longer that trip when it fires, it
   is dropped rather than retargeted at whatever is now open. Revision 2's `attemptSave` read `state.doc` at
   execution time, which is how trip A's pending write came to be executed against trip B.

   **Leaving the page is the same case, and the platform will not fully cooperate.** `apps/web` registers
   `visibilitychange` → `hidden` *and* `pagehide` (deduped) and calls `store.flush()` from both, and
   registers a `beforeunload` handler that calls `preventDefault()` while `isDirty()` so the browser shows
   its own "Leave site?" prompt. Verified, and stated as the limitation it is: `hidden` is the last state
   transition a page can reliably observe, `pagehide`/`beforeunload`/`unload` are *not* reliable on mobile,
   Safari does not always fire `visibilitychange` when the user clicks a link away, and the `beforeunload`
   dialog requires sticky activation — satisfied here by construction, since the user typed the edit.
   Crucially, an unload handler **cannot await an asynchronous IndexedDB write**, so the page-exit guarantee
   is "flushed at the last point the platform reliably offers, plus a native prompt if the user leaves
   dirty" — nothing stronger, and the criterion says so rather than pretending. The real guarantee is 6a/6b,
   which covers every in-app transition and needs no cooperation from the browser at all.

   **6d. And a transition is not a moment either** (revision 47, QA **R47-1** MAJOR, **R47-2** MAJOR).
   6a–6c guarantee that a pending write is flushed *before* the active document changes. They say nothing
   about the awaits that sit **between** the flush and the install — `openTrip`'s `ports.storage.load(id)`
   is one, `importDoc`'s id-minting loop is another — and everything dispatched inside that window is
   discarded by the install, with `persistence.status` reading `'idle'` over it. That is 6a″'s own
   sentence, *"a flush is not a moment"*, one frame further out than R5-1 read it: the loop re-asserts
   `dirty()` after every write and then hands the caller a **boolean**, which is a fact about an instant
   that has already passed by the time the caller acts on it. **The answer is `A-67` below: the flush stops
   returning a boolean and starts returning a ticket.** Read A-67 with 6a″ — it is what makes 6a's
   guarantee survive its own function's return, and it is the mechanism R47-2 needs as well.
   **And read A-68 with A-67** (revision 49, QA **R48-1**/**R48-2**): a ticket answers *which* install
   wins and says nothing about *whether* the operation it invalidated is ever replaced. The second half of
   6d is A-68 Part 3 — **a bump of a slot's sequence is a promise to replace the answer it invalidated**,
   and it is what keeps §10.6's *"exactly one terminal state follows every `'loading'`"* true.
   **And read A-69 with both** (revision 50, QA **R49-1**/**R49-5**): a promise is only as good as the
   place it is discharged, and A-68 discharged it by asking a *different* slot's ticket whether somebody
   else had answered. The third half of 6d is A-69 Part 3 — **no correctness argument in this store may
   rest on an enumeration of control-flow exits**; the promise is kept at a boundary every path must pass
   through, not at a list of sites a builder must remember.
   **And read A-70 last** (revision 51, BUILD-NOTES **KD-84**): a boundary is only as good as the question
   its predicate asks, and A-69's asked whether the *field* held an error rather than whether the *slot*
   had been bumped since the answer was written. The fourth half of 6d is A-70 Part 3 — **a predicate that
   decides whether an obligation is outstanding reads the record of the obligation, not a consequence of
   it** — and its mechanism is one stamp taken beside the one write.

#### A-67 — a flush is not a moment and neither is a transition: the store's generation guard (revision 47, QA **R47-1** MAJOR, **R47-2** MAJOR; ROADMAP **I-13d**)

> **STATUS: RULED, and it replaces two shipped point-fixes rather than layering over them.** One new
> module (`packages/client/src/store/generation.ts`, ~40 lines, no dependency), three guarded slots, five
> functions, two new message constants. **R46-1's `isLiveTrip(tripId)` and `state.doc?.id !== tripId`
> guards and R46-3's `state.doc?.id !== doc.id` guards are DELETED** — see Part 7. No `AppState` field, no
> selector, no port method, no persisted value, no type in `packages/core`, no `SCHEMA_VERSION`/
> `DB_VERSION`/`SUMMARY_VERSION` movement, and **no `.tsx`**.
>
> **Amended at revision 48 by Part 7a**, which narrows Part 7's *"every existing test stays exactly as it
> is"* to final-state assertions only. **Anyone reading Part 7 reads Part 7a with it.** Nothing else in
> this entry moves — no mechanism, no slot, no call site, no criterion.
>
> **Amended again at revision 49 by A-68**, immediately below, which corrects **three wiring defects at
> this entry's own call sites** and leaves the mechanism untouched (round 48 attacked it and could not
> break it — Part 3 stands entire). What moves: **Part 5**'s unconditional three-slot claim becomes a
> **one**-slot claim on `doc`, with `photoAvailability` and `browsing` **superseded at the reseed** that
> replaces them, because nine transition exits install nothing and were stranding an availability read
> for the trip that stayed open (QA **R48-2**); **Part 6**'s two `supersede('photoAvailability')` rows
> move **out of** R45-4's value guard and gain the answer they owe, and `deleteTrip` gains one line on its
> failure path (QA **R48-1**); **Part 7a** item 4's *"no other test changes"* is wrong for the second
> revision running and is replaced by a predicate (QA **R48-5**); and **Part 11 residue 4**'s
> *"unreachable from today's `apps/web`"* is **false** (QA **R48-3**). **Anyone reading Parts 4, 5, 6, 7a
> or 11 reads A-68 with them.**
>
> **Amended a third time at revision 50 by A-69**, at the end of this section. The mechanism *still* does
> not move — round 49 attacked it again and could not break it. What A-69 changes is the **shape of the
> argument**: A-68's fix for the nine exits was re-opened through its own discharge gate (QA **R49-1**), and
> an eleventh exit exists that no enumeration of *non*-installing exits could contain (QA **R49-5**), so
> **no correctness argument in this store may any longer rest on an enumeration of control-flow exits**
> (A-69 Part 3). Part 7's table and A-68 Part 4.1's table are demoted to documentation. **Anyone reading
> Part 7 or Part 11 reads A-69 Part 3 and Part 11 with them.**

**Part 1 — the two findings are one defect, and it is not in the photo code.**

R47-1 and R47-2 read as two bugs and are one. Both are **a guard that checks the right fact at a moment
that is not the right moment**, which is the breaker's own sentence and is exactly right.

- **R47-1.** `openTrip` is `await flushForTransition()` … `await ports.storage.load(id)` … `set(…,
  {reseed:true})`. Anything dispatched between the flush's return and the `set` lands in a document the
  `set` is about to replace. The record is gone, `dirty()` is false because `savedDoc` was reseeded
  alongside `doc`, and the indicator says `'idle'`. `importPhotos` is the only thing in this application
  that dispatches from a promise the user did not just create, so it is the reachable producer — but the
  window predates the photo arc entirely, and `setTripMeta` has the identical shape with no shipped
  surface reaching it. **Measured: four files picked, four decoded, four written to disk, three lost,
  `failures: []`, `pending: 0`.** Unbounded, because re-opening the **same** trip passes the
  `state.doc?.id === tripId` check on both sides of the transition, so every re-open swallows one more
  decode and the loop runs on.
- **R47-2.** `readPhotoAvailability`'s round-46 guard asks *"is this answer for the trip that is open?"*
  and never *"is this answer the newest one?"*, so two overlapping reads **for the same trip** still let
  the older land last. Three faces, all measured: a double-tap producing R45-4's exact defect
  (`'missing'` over bytes on disk); an older `refreshPhotoAvailability` landing after `doMerge`'s read,
  which is **R46-2's own measured end state on R46-2's own fix**; and a successful *Try again* reverted to
  `'unreadable'` by the failing read that preceded it.

The common structure: **an actor captures a fact about the store, awaits, and then writes on the strength
of the captured fact.** Trip identity is not that fact. It is a *proxy* for it, and a proxy that is true
of two different states — the outgoing document and the incoming one for the same id; the older read's
subject and the newer read's — is a guarantee that reads true and measures false. §2.9 A-47 Part 2 made
the same correction one subject over (*"stop proxying and start recording"*), and §0.6 is the same
principle again: *a fact about a resource is only valid at the moment, and in the place, the resource
itself stated it.* **This ruling is §0.6 applied to the store's own in-flight operations**, which is the
one place four rounds have now found it unapplied.

**Part 2 — the fix R47-1 names is refused, and refusing it is most of the reason this entry exists.**

R47-1's *"The fix, and it is small"* paragraph offers two shapes. Both are refused, and a builder must
not take either.

1. **"Move `flushForTransition()` to just before the `set`."** This **creates** a defect worse than the
   one it closes. Walk it: the flush writes the in-memory document (with the record) at expectation *V₁*,
   so storage advances to *V₂*, `savedVersion` becomes *V₂*. The `set` then installs `stored.doc` — read
   at *V₁*, without the record — **and `persistence.savedVersion: stored.version`, which is *V₁***. Memory
   now holds the older document, storage holds the newer one, and the fence points at a version storage
   left two writes ago. The next keystroke's autosave expects *V₁*, is refused, and the tab displays
   *"Not saved — edited elsewhere"* with **no other writer to merge with** — §4.2 rule 4's own
   "unresolvable rather than recoverable" state, manufactured by the fix. This is §2.2b F2 broken by a
   flush, which is the one function in this file that exists to uphold it.
2. **"Re-run it if the document moved."** This one is *correct* and is still refused. To be correct it
   must re-run the **load** as well — otherwise it installs the stale `stored` over the freshly written
   document and lands on defect (1) — so it is `{flush; load}` in a loop, which needs its own bound, its
   own exhausted exit and its own three-way re-arm rule, all of which 6a″ spent a whole revision getting
   right for the flush alone. It doubles the storage round trips on every contested navigation. **And it
   does nothing at all for R47-2**, or for any future async writer, so the next round finds the fifth
   face.

**The correct fix is not to make writes in the window survive. It is to make the window unwritable, and
to give every in-flight operation a way to know it is in one.** That is one mechanism, it closes both
findings, and it closes them for `setTripMeta`, `adoptTrip`, `importDoc`, `browseTrip` and every future
operation of the same shape without any of them being named.

**Part 3 — the mechanism, in full. One module, five functions, no dependency.**

`packages/client/src/store/generation.ts`:

```ts
/** A slot of store state whose replacement must be ordered. See A-67 Part 4 for the criterion. */
export type GuardedSlot = 'doc' | 'browsing' | 'photoAvailability';

/** Opaque, monotone, per slot, per store instance. Ephemeral — A-67 Part 9. */
export type Ticket = number;

export interface GenerationGuard {
  /** "I am going to REPLACE this slot." Invalidates every ticket issued for it before now.
   *  Pair with `release` in a `finally`. */
  claim(slot: GuardedSlot): Ticket;
  /** Ends a claim. ALWAYS in a `finally`, on every exit including the throws. */
  release(slot: GuardedSlot): void;
  /** "I am going to write THROUGH this slot, not replace it." `null` while a claim is open —
   *  a ticket taken inside somebody else's window would not be invalidated by their install. */
  observe(slot: GuardedSlot): Ticket | null;
  /** THE predicate. Is this ticket still the newest issued for its slot? */
  current(slot: GuardedSlot, t: Ticket | null): boolean;
  /** A SYNCHRONOUS replacement of a slot, which has no window: invalidate, then write. */
  supersede(slot: GuardedSlot): void;
}

export function createGenerationGuard(): GenerationGuard {
  const seq: Record<GuardedSlot, number> = { doc: 0, browsing: 0, photoAvailability: 0 };
  const busy: Record<GuardedSlot, number> = { doc: 0, browsing: 0, photoAvailability: 0 };
  return {
    claim: (s) => { busy[s]++; return ++seq[s]; },
    release: (s) => { busy[s]--; },
    observe: (s) => (busy[s] > 0 ? null : seq[s]),
    current: (s, t) => t !== null && seq[s] === t,
    supersede: (s) => { seq[s]++; },
  };
}
```

Four things about this that are the ruling and not the implementation:

1. **`current` is one comparison and does not consult `busy`, and that is a proof rather than an
   oversight.** An observation is only ever issued when `busy === 0`, and every claim increments `seq`,
   so if any claim has been made since an observation was taken then `seq !== t` **whether or not that
   claim has settled**. The `busy` counter is needed by `observe` and by nothing else. A builder who adds
   `busy[s] === 0` to `current` breaks the claimer's own write, because a claimer's window is open at the
   moment it checks its own ticket.
2. **`observe` returning `null` is load-bearing, not defensive.** An operation that takes a ticket
   *inside* a transition's window would capture the value that transition has already minted, would still
   hold it after the install, and would write into a document it never saw. `null` makes that
   unrepresentable; `current(slot, null)` is `false` by the first clause.
3. **It is created inside `createStore`, per store instance.** The counters are closure state, never
   module state. Two stores over one `memoryStorage` is this project's standard two-tab fixture and they
   must not share a sequence.
4. **`Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` is not a bound anyone reaches.** At one transition per millisecond for the
   life of the process it is ~285,000 years. Stated so it is a checked assumption and not an unexamined
   one; no wraparound handling ships.

**The one assumption it rests on** is ECMAScript run-to-completion: between a synchronous `current(...)`
check and the synchronous statement after it, nothing else in this agent runs. That is the same
assumption `attemptSave`'s `forTripId` drop, `doMerge`'s in-link `state.doc !== doc` check and `set()`'s
five steps already make, three times over in this file. It is why **every check in Part 6 is the last
statement before its write, with no `await` between them** — a check separated from its act by an await
is the check-then-act §0.6 forbids, and re-introducing one is how this ruling gets a fifth face.

**Part 4 — the three slots, and the criterion that decides whether a fourth is needed.**

> **A store field needs a guarded slot when an asynchronous operation installs a value into it that was
> computed from a snapshot taken before an `await`. A field written from `state` at the instant of writing
> does not need one, and must not get one.**

That criterion, applied to every field an async path in `store.ts` writes:

| Field | Written from | Slot? |
|---|---|---|
| `doc` / `activeTripId` / `persistence` / `history` / `ui` — the reseed set | a `Trip` loaded, parsed or built before the install | **`doc`**. All six of rule 6a's transitions replace them together and claim together |
| `browsing` | `browseTrip`'s pre-await `load` | **`browsing`**. Two overlapping browses let the older pane win, and `copyStopInto` reads that pane |
| `photos.tripId` / `photos.available` / `photos.availabilityError` | a `present()` answer issued before the await | **`photoAvailability`** |
| `photos.pending` / `photos.total` | `state.photos.pending ± n`, read at write time | no — R45-11 already made these read-modify-write, and that is the criterion's other half |
| `photos.failures` | `[...state.photos.failures, …]`, read at write time | no |
| `photos.orphans` | `state.photos.orphans.filter/…`, read at write time | no |
| `library` (`upsertSummary`, `runRescan`'s link) | `state.library`, read at write time, inside `chainOntoSaving` | no — the chain already gives these a total order |
| `openFailures` | `state.openFailures`, read at write time | no |
| `rescan` | `state.rescan`, read at write time | no |
| `library` (`refreshLibrary`) | `listTrips()` issued before the await | **not now** — Part 11 residue 1 states the case and its trigger |

**A transition claims all three slots**, because a reseed replaces all three, and because "the fields a
reseed replaces" is a rule a builder can apply without judgement. It never *checks* `browsing` or
`photoAvailability`: those claims exist to invalidate other people's in-flight work, which is the second
half of the rule —

> **A write that changes the subject an in-flight read is reading must invalidate that read.** A byte
> `write` or `remove` changes what `present()` would answer, so the synchronous `setPhotos({available})`
> that follows one calls `supersede('photoAvailability')` first — not to protect itself, but to stop an
> availability read issued *before* those bytes existed from landing *after* them and reporting
> `'missing'` over them. That is R45-4 reached through a third door and it is closed by one call.

*(**Amended at revision 49 — A-68 Part 5, QA R48-1.** The rule above is right and unconditional; Part 6's
**placement** of the call was not. It shipped **inside** R45-4's `available !== null` value guard, so it did
not fire in the one case that needed it. A-68 hoists it out and keeps R45-4's guard nested inside it — and
adds the half this paragraph never states: **the invalidated read must be replaced.** A supersede that
cannot write the answer itself owes a port read. A-68 Part 3.)*

**Part 5 — where the claim happens, and why it is inside `flushForTransition` rather than on the
transition's first line.**

This is the subtlest part of the ruling and getting it wrong re-opens R47-1 in a narrower form.

**The claim may not go on the transition's first line.** A dispatch that lands *during* the flush is not
lost today — 6a″'s loop re-asserts `dirty()` after every write and writes it, and `openTrip`'s subsequent
`load` reads it straight back. Claiming first would make `dispatch` refuse an edit that currently
survives correctly. That is a regression against R5-1, paid to fix R5-1's successor.

**The claim may not go on the line after the flush either.** `if (!(await flushForTransition())) …`
resumes in a microtask, and a `derive` promise resolving in exactly that gap dispatches after the loop's
last `dirty()` read and before the caller's first statement. The gap is small and it is the same kind of
gap this ruling exists to close.

**So the claim is the flush's own last synchronous act, in the same block as the `dirty()` read it is
attesting to.** `flushForTransition` changes signature:

```ts
/** §4.2 rule 6a/6a″, and rule 6d's ticket (A-67). `null` is rule 6b's refusal. */
async function flushForTransition(): Promise<Ticket | null> {
  for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
    const timerPending = cancelPending !== null;
    cancelTimer();
    const idle = state.persistence.status === 'idle';
    const skip = idle && !timerPending && !dirty();
    if (!state.doc || skip) return claimTransition();   // ← the claim, beside the dirty() read
    if (attempt >= FLUSH_MAX_ATTEMPTS) { /* unchanged */ return null; }
    await save();
    await saving;
    const { status } = state.persistence;
    if (status === 'conflict' || status === 'error') return null;
  }
}

/** SUPERSEDED at revision 49 — A-68 Part 4. Both bodies below are now ONE line: the `doc` slot only.
 *  The other two are `supersede`d at the reseed. Do not build the version below. */
function claimTransition(): Ticket {
  guard.claim('browsing');             // ← deleted at A-68
  guard.claim('photoAvailability');    // ← deleted at A-68
  return guard.claim('doc');           // the ticket callers hold and check
}
/** The ONE place a live-document transition ends. Always in a `finally`. */
function releaseTransition(): void {
  guard.release('doc');
  guard.release('photoAvailability');  // ← deleted at A-68
  guard.release('browsing');           // ← deleted at A-68
}
```

**That is the whole of the generalisation, stated in one sentence:** R5-1 made the flush re-assert
`dirty()` after every write; A-67 makes the **answer** it returns carry an expiry. A `true` said *"there
was nothing unwritten a moment ago"*; a ticket says *"there is nothing unwritten now, and here is how you
will know when that stops being true."*

**`flushForTransition` claims unconditionally, with no opt-out parameter, and that costs one deliberate
false positive.** `deleteTrip` of a **non**-active trip flushes but installs no document, so its claim
needlessly invalidates an import in flight for the trip that *is* active — the batch stops, having kept
and persisted everything it had already dispatched. The alternative is a parameter that lets a caller opt
out of the guarantee, and **rule 6a′ is this document's own record of what an opt-out on this exact
function costs**: the skip that existed to avoid rewriting 176 KB is where the whole of rule 6 was lost.
One conservative stop on a rare gesture is the cheaper failure, and it is disclosed rather than
discovered.

*(**Superseded in part at revision 49 — A-68 Part 4, QA R48-2.** `flushForTransition` still claims
unconditionally with no opt-out parameter, and the deliberate false positive above is unchanged — but it
claims **`doc` only**. `claimTransition()` no longer claims `photoAvailability` or `browsing`: **nine** of
its exits install no document and issue no replacement read, so a claim on either was a promise nine paths
do not keep, and the cost was §10.6 property 5's unresolving spinner on the trip that stayed open. Those
two slots are **superseded at the reseed that replaces them**, which is where Part 4's own criterion puts
them.)*

**Part 6 — every call site, exhaustively. This table is the builder's contract.**

> **Four rows of this table are amended at revision 49 by A-68 and a fifth gains a line — read it before
> implementing any of them.** `flushForTransition`/`claimTransition` claim **`doc` only** and the six
> reseed installs gain `supersede('photoAvailability')` + `supersede('browsing')` (A-68 Part 4);
> `importPhotos`' and `removePhoto`'s `supersede` rows move **out of** R45-4's value guard and gain the
> owed read, and `removePhoto` gains a `guard.observe('doc')` it never had (A-68 Part 5); `deleteTrip`
> gains one `readPhotoAvailability` on the exit where its cascade rejects (A-68 Part 6). Everything else
> in the table below is unchanged and correct.

| Function | What it does | Checks? |
|---|---|---|
| `flushForTransition` | returns `claimTransition()` on both success exits (`!state.doc` and `skip`), `null` on all three refusals | — |
| `createTrip` | `const t = await flushForTransition(); if (t === null) return state;` … `if (!guard.current('doc', t)) throw new Error(TRANSITION_SUPERSEDED_MESSAGE);` immediately before the `set` … `finally { releaseTransition(); }` … `readPhotoAvailability` and `save()` **after** the release | **yes — throws** |
| `adoptTrip` | the same; the `finally` covers the `this.openTrip(doc.id)` delegation, whose own nested claim is correct and settles first | **yes — throws** |
| `openTrip` | the same, except the supersession **returns `state`** and installs nothing; `noteOpenFailure` and the rethrow are unchanged and stay inside the window | **yes — returns** |
| `closeTrip` | the same as `openTrip` | **yes — returns** |
| `importDoc` | the same; the window covers `fromJSON`, the ownership refusal and the whole id-minting loop; `save()` and `readPhotoAvailability` go **after** the release | **yes — throws** |
| `deleteTrip` | **does not use `flushForTransition` on the active branch.** `if (state.activeTripId === id) { cancelTimer(); claimTransition(); } else if ((await flushForTransition()) === null) return state;` — then the existing body, then `finally { releaseTransition(); }` | **no** |
| `browseTrip` | `const t = guard.claim('browsing')` on line 1 (it does not flush and never has); `if (!guard.current('browsing', t)) return doc;` immediately before the `set`; `finally { guard.release('browsing'); }`. `noteOpenFailure` and the rethrow are unchanged | **yes — returns the parsed doc** |
| `closeBrowse` | `guard.supersede('browsing')` immediately before its `set` | — |
| `readPhotoAvailability` | `const t = guard.claim('photoAvailability')` on line 1, before every branch; **every** `setPhotos` in the function gated by `guard.current('photoAvailability', t)`; `finally { guard.release('photoAvailability'); }` | **yes — returns** |
| `importPhotos` | `const g = guard.observe('doc')` beside the existing `const tripId = state.doc.id`, **before** `pickImages()`; `if (g === null) return state;` there; `if (!guard.current('doc', g)) return state;` immediately after `pickImages()` resolves and **before** `pending`/`total` move; `if (!guard.current('doc', g)) break;` at **both** loop guards | **yes — breaks** |
| `importPhotos`' optimistic `setPhotos({available})` | `guard.supersede('photoAvailability')` immediately before it | — |
| `removePhoto`'s `setPhotos({available})` | `guard.supersede('photoAvailability')` immediately before it | — |
| `dispatch` / `undo` / `redo` | refuse while a `doc` claim is open: `throw new Error(TRANSITION_IN_PROGRESS_MESSAGE)` as the first statement | **yes — throws** |

**Two message constants, exported beside `CONFLICT_MESSAGE` and `FLUSH_EXHAUSTED_MESSAGE`:**

```ts
export const TRANSITION_SUPERSEDED_MESSAGE =
  'Another trip was opened while this one was being prepared. Nothing was changed — try again.';
export const TRANSITION_IN_PROGRESS_MESSAGE =
  'A trip is being opened or closed; that edit was not applied. Try again in a moment.';
```

**Why a supersession throws for a creation and returns for a navigation**, since it is the one place this
table exercises judgement, and the split is a rule rather than a list:

- **A navigation** — `openTrip`, `closeTrip`, `browseTrip` — aborts silently, and the abort is honest
  because *the outcome is on the screen*: a newer transition is installing, and what the user is about to
  see is what their newest gesture asked for. This is A-66 Part 5 item 3's standard, and it is the exact
  case R6-1 distinguished from: R6-1's silent abort left the user on an unchanged screen with no
  explanation, which is why the flush's bound-exhausted exit had to grow a banner.
- **A creation** — `createTrip`, `adoptTrip`, `importDoc` — throws, because nothing else on the screen
  will show that the creation did not happen. All three have a caller that awaits and can render an
  error; `openTrip` already throws on this path for a corrupt document and both of its callers handle it.
- **A `deleteTrip` never checks**, because its install is computed from `state` at the instant of writing
  (`if (state.activeTripId === id)`), which is Part 4's criterion answering the question for it. It still
  claims: the delete must invalidate an availability read and an import for a trip it is destroying, and
  R46-1 face 3's requirement — *no byte record written for a file that had not reached its `write`* — is
  now met by the same check as everything else. **The `ports.storage.delete` and the library-row removal
  are never conditional on a ticket**; only a document *install* is.

**Part 7 — how this subsumes R46-1's and R46-3's point-fixes. Both are DELETED, not layered under.**

This is stated site by site so a builder does not have to guess, and the guessing is the risk: a weaker
check left beside a stronger one that runs at the same instant adds nothing and is how round 46's readers
came to believe the case was closed.

| Shipped guard | Verdict | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `importPhotos` `if (!isLiveTrip(tripId)) break;` (step 4, R46-1) | **replaced** by `if (!guard.current('doc', g)) break;` | The only way a live batch's trip can be deleted is `deleteTrip` of the **active** trip, which claims. A batch cannot be live for a non-active trip: opening any other trip claims and breaks it first. So the generation check is strictly stronger — and it fires **before the decode's `write`** rather than after it, which is what closes A-66 Part 7's orphan for the common case (Part 8). |
| `isLiveTrip` itself | **deleted** | `:1511` is its only caller. |
| `importPhotos` `if (state.doc?.id !== tripId) break;` (step 5, R46-1) | **replaced** by the same `guard.current('doc', g)` check | Identity by id is true of two different document instances for one trip, which is R47-1 face 3 in one sentence. `tripId` itself **stays** — it is the byte key, it is captured in the same synchronous block as the ticket, and the two therefore agree by construction. |
| `readPhotoAvailability` `if (state.doc?.id !== doc.id) return;` on **both** branches (R46-3) | **replaced** by `if (!guard.current('photoAvailability', t)) return;` on both | The cross-trip case R46-3 was written for is covered because every replacement of `state.doc` claims `photoAvailability`; the same-trip case it could not see is covered because every read claims its own ticket. The old check cannot be kept as belt-and-braces: it is not weaker-but-independent, it is the *same* check with a coarser key, and it is false in exactly one direction — it passes when the answer is stale. |
| `importPhotos` `if (state.photos.available !== null && state.photos.tripId === state.doc.id)` (R45-4) | **kept, unchanged**, with a `supersede('photoAvailability')` added immediately before the `setPhotos` inside it | R45-4's guard answers a different question — *"was availability ever read for this trip"* — which no ticket encodes and which `null` still means. Part 4's table is why: `available !== null` is a fact about the value, not about the ordering. |
| `removePhoto`'s `if (state.photos.available !== null)` | **kept, unchanged**, same `supersede` addition | Same reason. |
| `attemptSave`'s `forTripId !== null && doc.id !== forTripId` (R3-2) | **kept, unchanged** | It guards a *timer*, which holds no ticket and never will; §4.2 rule 6c calls it belt and braces and it stays that. |
| `doMerge`'s `if (state.doc !== doc)` inside its `chainOntoSaving` link (R11-1) | **kept, unchanged, and it is the precedent** | Reference identity on the document, checked inside the link with no await before the act. It is already what this ruling generalises, which is why a merge is **not** a transition and claims nothing: a dispatch landing inside a merge causes the *merge* to yield, and the edit survives. |

**How the builder proves the subsumption rather than asserting it: the existing tests are not deleted.**
~~Every test written for R46-1 and R46-3 stays exactly as it is, and must be green with the point-fixes
removed and the generation guard in.~~ *(**Narrowed at revision 48** — the blanket form was wrong by
exactly one assertion and **Part 7a** replaces this sentence. The corrected claim: **every test written for
R46-1 and R46-3 that asserts a FINAL STATE stays exactly as it is** — which trip a record lands in, what
phase a listing reports, what `pending`/`total`/`failures` settle to, and whether a byte pair is readable
by the trip that holds it. **The one assertion that moves is the one that pins the OLD guard's byte-write
side effect**, and it moves because the new mechanism writes fewer bytes, not more.)* A test that only
passes because of a guard being deleted is a test measuring the guard instead of the behaviour, and it is
the builder's job to report that rather than to adjust it. **The I-13d builder did exactly that at
`4316167` and this Part is the answer.**

**Part 7a — the one existing assertion that moves, and it moves because the fix landed (revision 48; the
I-13d builder's report against `4316167`, and ROADMAP **G3**).**

**The contradiction, in one sentence.** Part 7's blanket *"stays exactly as it is"* and ROADMAP I-13d's
ship-gate criterion **G3** (*"zero stranded derivative pairs: the break precedes the byte `write`.
Mutation: restore `isLiveTrip(tripId)` at the step-4 guard → one pair stranded → red"*) make **opposite**
predictions about the identical scenario — a trip transition landing during `derive`. They cannot both
hold, because **the R46-1 test's expected value is literally the G3 mutant's expected red output.**

**The mechanics, confirmed against the shipped code and not inferred.** In `importPhotos`,
`if (!guard.current('doc', g)) break;` is the statement **immediately before**
`await ports.photo.write(tripId, id, derived.thumb.bytes, derived.display.bytes)` — the step-4 guard fires
**before** the write, where the deleted `isLiveTrip(tripId)` fired **after** it. So under a transition that
lands inside the decode, the abandoned file's byte pair is **never created**. This is not "written and then
swept": there is no write, no cleanup, no window. Both artifacts below observe `[]` where they were written
to observe one key, and that empty array is the whole of the difference.

**The ruling. G3 is correct and Part 7's blanket claim is narrowed, in that order and not the other.**

1. **Fewer photographs lost is the outcome this ruling exists to produce.** §10 **A-66 Part 10** item 2
   already says it in as many words — *"the common case now strands nothing at all… Part 7's orphan is no
   longer produced by the case Part 7 was written about"* — and A-67 Part 7's own `isLiveTrip` row says
   *"it fires **before the decode's `write`** rather than after it."* The architecture has asserted the new
   behaviour in two places since revision 47. The only thing that did not get updated was the sentence
   claiming no test would notice.
2. **A test that pins a defect's collateral damage is not protecting a contract.** The old assertion's
   subject is *where the orphan went*, and an orphan that is not produced has nowhere to go. The contract
   R46-1 was written to protect is **"the record does not land in the trip the user switched to, and no
   listing reports `'ready'` over bytes another trip holds"** — and every assertion of *that* in both
   artifacts is green under A-67, unedited. Only the collateral clause moves.
3. **So the narrowed claim, stated so nobody re-derives it:** *no existing test asserting a **final state**
   moves — which trip a record lands in, a listing's phase, `pending`/`total`/`failures`, readability. The
   one existing assertion pinning the **old guard's byte-write side effect** — that exactly **one**
   derivative pair gets stranded rather than **zero** — **must be updated**, because the new mechanism
   makes those bytes never get written at all. That is a strictly better outcome and not a regression the
   old assertion should be allowed to protect.* **Its inversion is the proof that A-67 landed**, which is
   what G3 is for, and it is the only assertion in this repository with that property.
4. **Nothing else in Part 7 moves.** Every row of Part 7's table stands, the four kept guards stay kept,
   and the deletions are the deletions. ~~**No other test, in `packages/client/test/` or in `qa/`, changes
   for this**~~ — a builder who finds a second one has found something this ruling did not, and reports it
   rather than editing it. *(**The struck sentence is FALSE and is corrected at revision 49 — A-68 Part 9,
   QA R48-5.** Three more `qa/` assertions move — `qa/r47-i13c.mjs:210`, `:231` and `:263` — and one of
   them is a **final-state** assertion, which item 3 above says does not happen. It is the `A → B → A`
   return trip, it is correct behaviour, and it moved because the old guard got the right answer by the
   mechanism that lost photographs elsewhere. **This is the second consecutive revision to under-count
   this blast radius, so A-68 Part 9 replaces the enumeration with a predicate and requires the list to be
   derived by running the probes.** The reporting instruction in the surviving half of this item stands
   and is what the round-48 breaker correctly followed.)*

**The exact corrections owed, one per artifact, and they are the same single observable.**

| Artifact | Now asserts | Must assert | Whose hand |
|---|---|---|---|
| `packages/client/test/photos.test.ts:864` (test *"R46-1: a trip switch mid-decode does not file the record in the trip the user switched to"*) | `deepEqual([...p.photo.thumbs.keys()], [photoByteKey(A, 'photo-1')])`, described as *"the bytes belong to the trip the files were picked from, and stay there"* | `deepEqual([...p.photo.thumbs.keys()], [])`, described as **"no bytes are written at all for a file whose decode outlives the trip it was picked from — the guard precedes the `write` (A-67 Part 7a, ROADMAP G3)"**. **`display`'s key set is asserted empty beside it**, since the same `write` call produces both and an assertion over one store only is how a half-write goes unseen. **The process question, ruled: `qa/` is the breaker's, and a builder does not touch it even when the
correction is one line and obvious.** This is settled convention in this arc and revision 48 does not
invent it, it applies it:

- **Round 44.** The I-12a builder left `qa/r43-a56.mjs` §E/§F/§M red rather than re-cut them, and wrote the
  reason down: *"editing an adversarial probe so it reports my own fix as green is the move that must not
  be made quietly by the person fixing it."* That was correct then and is the same move now.
- **Revision 44 → round 46.** Six lines of `qa/r45-i13.mjs` asserted round 45's *proposed* fixes rather than
  revision 44's chosen ones. The I-13b builder refused the edit (zero-line diff) and **round 46's breaker**

- **Revision 46 → round 47.** **A-65 Part 8** names `qa/r46-i13b.mjs` §K and `qa/r45-i13.mjs` §K and says

So: **`packages/client/test/photos.test.ts:864` is builder work** — it is the suite's own test of the
suite's own behaviour, and the builder who changed the behaviour owns the assertion that measures it.
**`qa/r46-i13b.mjs:259` is breaker work** and is **flagged for the next breaker pass** (the round that
confirms I-13d), not queued for a builder. Two consequences a reader needs:

1. **`qa/r46-i13b.mjs` printing one `FAIL` at the I-13d gate is an expected, disclosed result and not a
   ship condition** — ROADMAP I-13d's *"the two probes green unedited"* line is narrowed by revision 48 to
   exclude this one line, and only this one. A `FAIL` on **any other** line of either probe is still a
   regression and still blocks.
2. **The re-cut carries a vacuity control**, as round 47's did: the inverted line must be watched **red**
   against a build with `isLiveTrip(tripId)` restored at the step-4 guard, which is G3's own mutant. An
   assertion that `keys(p)` is empty passes trivially against a probe that never imported anything, and
   the control is what separates the two.

**Part 8 — what deliberately gets no guard, named so a builder does not add one.**

1. **`retireResolutions`' `set` from inside `getDerived()`.** A subscriber rendering during a transition
   window can reach it, and its `set` would be discarded by the install. That is harmless and stays
   unguarded: `retiredAt` is bookkeeping re-derived from the arriving document by `set`'s own reseed
   branch (§2.7 A-5 step 2), and the `scheduleSave()` it arms is either dropped by `attemptSave`'s
   `forTripId` or writes the newly installed document, both of which are correct. Examined, not
   overlooked.
2. **`noteOpenFailure`'s `set` inside a transition window.** `openFailures` is library-scoped, carried
   across every reseed, and written from `state` at the instant of writing. Part 4's criterion says no.
3. **`setUi`.** It writes no guarded field. A UI selection lost to a transition is not data loss, and
   `initialState()` resets `ui` on every transition anyway.
4. **The `chainOntoSaving` links.** `runRescan`, `deleteTrip`'s delete link and every `writeAndSettle`
   already have a total order from the chain, which is a stronger property than a ticket. §4.3's grep is
   unchanged and no `ports.storage.*` call moves.
5. **`reclaimPhotoBytes`.** Its subject is ids that are *not* in `state.doc.photos`, so no `present()`
   query set contains them and no availability read is stale because of it. No `supersede`.
6. **`exportActive` / `exportStoredDoc` / `refreshLibrary` / `rescanSummaries` / `flush` / `isDirty` /
   `getState` / `getDerived` / `subscribe` / `syncResolutions` / `clearMergeNotice` /
   `dismissPhotoFailures`.** None installs a value computed before an await into a guarded slot.
   `refreshLibrary` is the one with a real ordering question and it is Part 11 residue 1, not this
   increment.
7. **`packages/core`.** Nothing here reaches it. Core has no async operations and no store.

**Part 9 — the classification: ephemeral session state, and confirming that is the right one.**

The counters are **not persisted, not exported, not in `AppState`, not in `history`, and not in
`toJSON`.** Four reasons, and the fourth is the one that matters:

1. Nothing survives a reload holding a ticket, so a persisted counter would be restored beside zero live
   holders and would mean nothing. There is no fact about the *trip* here.
2. In `AppState` it would have to be carried or reset at every reseed site — which is the carry-or-reset
   decision that `rescan`/`openFailures` get right and that A-66 Part 3 shows `PhotoSession` gets right
   for the opposite reason. A third answer to that question is a third chance to get it wrong.
3. In `AppState` it would be inside `history`'s snapshots, so `undo` would restore a **generation**. That
   is R8-1's defect class exactly.
4. **In `AppState` a subscriber could render off it**, and there is no honest thing to render: "a
   transition is in progress" is a fact about a window measured in milliseconds. If a future surface ever
   needs to disable editing during a transition, that is a new derived signal with its own ruling — not a
   counter leaked onto a screen.

This is the same classification `merging`, `rescanning`, `saving`, `cache` and `cancelPending` already
carry: module-private closure state inside `createStore`, invisible to `AppState`, asserted only through
behaviour. **The "derived not stored" discipline is satisfied by construction** — a generation is neither
derived nor stored; it is a fact about an operation, and operations are not part of the model.

**Part 10 — the injected-fault criteria, because §0.5 applies to every rule here. Nine, and every one is
red before and green after.**

| | Fault | Required behaviour |
|---|---|---|

G1–G7 are behavioural and belong in `packages/client/test/`; G8 and G9 are the A-64 **S5**-shaped
"still true" greps that make a refusal checkable rather than merely written.

**Part 11 — the residues, four, disclosed rather than left to be discovered.**

1. **`refreshLibrary` installs a `listTrips()` answer taken before its await, and has no slot.** Two
   overlapping calls let the older library win, and a delete landing in between can put a deleted row
   back — which is **R26-1**, closed for `runRescan`'s own re-read by putting it on the chain and not
   closed here. It is out of scope because `App.tsx` calls it once on boot and nothing else calls it
   concurrently today. **Trigger:** a second caller of `refreshLibrary`, or any surface that refreshes the
   library on a gesture — at which point the answer is a `'library'` slot on this same guard, or the
   chain, and it is one line either way.
2. **A `deleteTrip` of a non-active trip stops an import running for the active one.** Part 5's
   deliberate false positive. **Trigger:** a measured report of it, at which point the answer is *not* an
   opt-out parameter on `flushForTransition` (rule 6a′) but a fourth slot separating "the document is
   being replaced" from "some document is being flushed".
3. **A user who re-opens the trip they are importing into now stops the import**, where before they lost
   photographs silently and the loop ran on. Strictly better and still not good: the reachable producer is
   `App.tsx` calling `openTrip` unconditionally from the Map and Profile tabs, including for the trip that
   is **already active**, which is a navigation and not a document transition. **Trigger:** the next
   increment that opens `App.tsx` — it makes that call conditional on `state.activeTripId !== id`, which
   removes the whole scenario at the surface. That is a `.tsx` change and it is deliberately not in
   I-13d, which is fenced out of `.tsx` like the rest of this arc. §10 **A-66** Part 6's owed sentence is
   widened at revision 47 to cover it in the meantime. *(**Widened at revision 49 — A-68 Part 9, QA
   R48-5.** The same cost is paid by **`A → B → A`**, a user who leaves an importing trip and comes back,
   and the `.tsx` change named above does **not** remove that one. Measured: the batch stops and files
   nothing, reported as nothing per §10 **A-66 Part 3** — whose reason, *"the report would land against
   whatever trip the user moved to"*, is true of a batch abandoned **into** another trip and false of one
   abandoned by a round trip that returns. A-68 Part 9 scopes A-66 Part 3 rather than overturning it and
   hands the report question to the increment that builds the photo surface.)*
4. ~~**`dispatch`/`undo`/`redo` refusing during a window is unreachable from today's `apps/web`**~~ —
   ~~the round-47 breaker confirmed no editable field is mounted on any surface that calls `openTrip`. It
   ships as a **fence**, and its first user-visible appearance would be a surface that lets a user type
   while a transition is in flight.~~ **FALSE, and corrected at revision 49 — A-68 Part 8 (QA R48-3).**
   The round-47 confirmation answered a narrower question than this residue asked: the reachable caller is
   **not a field**. `apps/web/src/App.tsx:232–243` binds Ctrl/Cmd+Z on **`window`**, for the whole app,
   with no trip check and **no `try`**, and `deleteTrip` holds its `doc` claim across a cascade during
   which the active trip stays interactive — so a keyboard undo during a trip delete reaches this refusal
   **today**, as an uncaught throw inside a DOM event listener where no error boundary can see it. **The
   refusal itself is ruled correct and does not change** (A-68 Part 8 refuses both a silent no-op and a
   queued undo, with reasons); what is owed is a two-line `catch` in `App.tsx`, scheduled into the first
   increment that opens that file — ROADMAP **I-13e**'s `.tsx` follow-up, alongside residue 3's own.

**The trigger that reopens this ruling**, stated so it is a decision and not a wall: **a store operation
that must survive a transition rather than be dropped by one.** Every line above rests on *dropped, never
retargeted* — R3-2's rule for a late timer, A-66's rule for an abandoned batch, R46-3's rule for a losing
read. An operation whose work genuinely cannot be re-done by the user (a native background import, a
server sync applying a remote change) breaks that premise, and its increment decides where such work is
parked and re-applied — in one ruling, and not on the way to something else.

#### A-68 — a claim is a promise to answer: the wiring A-67 left at its own call sites (revision 49, QA **R48-1** MAJOR, **R48-2** MAJOR, **R48-3** MINOR, **R48-5** MINOR; ROADMAP **I-13e**)

> **STATUS: RULED. The mechanism is not on trial and does not move.** `packages/client/src/store/generation.ts`
> does not change **by a character** — no new slot, no new method, no signature change, no new module, no new
> type, no `AppState` field, no selector, no port method, no persisted value, nothing in `packages/core`, no
> `SCHEMA_VERSION`/`DB_VERSION`/`SUMMARY_VERSION` movement, and **no `.tsx`**. Everything below is
> `packages/client/src/store/store.ts` plus the tests that measure it.
>
> **What moves in A-67:** Part 5's three-slot claim becomes a **one**-slot claim; Part 6's `claimTransition`,
> `importPhotos`-supersede, `removePhoto`-supersede and `deleteTrip` rows; Part 7a item 4's blast-radius
> claim; Part 11 residue 4's *"unreachable"*. **Anyone reading A-67 Parts 4, 5, 6, 7a or 11 reads this entry
> with them.**
>
> **AMENDED AT REVISION 50 BY A-69** (QA **R49-1** MAJOR, **R49-2**…**R49-5** MINOR), at the end of this
> section, and it is the entry to read first if you are implementing anything from here. **Part 5b's and
> 5c's `availabilityOwed` flag and both of its discharge lines are DELETED** — the discharge was gated on
> the **`doc`** slot, which is the slot the nine exits of Part 4.1 all bump, so seven of the nine were
> re-opened by the fix for the other half of the same finding. **Part 4.1's table is demoted from proof to
> documentation**, Part 7's enumerated proof is **replaced** by a boundary argument, Part 4.2 item 1 gains a
> `browsing` clause (QA R49-4), Part 9's *"§K is green"* is **false** and corrected, and Part 10's **G14**
> and **G17** are corrected to describe faults that actually reproduce (QA R49-3). **Everything Part 4.2,
> Part 5a, Part 5c's `observe`/gate and Part 6 build STAYS** — A-69 removes the liveness half only.

**Part 1 — what round 48 established, and why this entry is short on argument.**

Round 48 threw the battery A-67 was written to survive at the mechanism itself and could not break it: a
four-transition sequence around a live four-file import, three `openTrip`s answering in the worst order, two
browses against a close and against a transition, two async writers on one slot, and a **nine**-case release
battery covering every throwing exit. Every slot always releases; the newest claim always wins. **Part 3's
four properties hold under attack and are not re-litigated here.**

Both MAJORs are in what A-67 asked *callers* to do with the mechanism, and both are the same missing
sentence. A-67 reasoned about **ordering** — which of two answers wins — for eleven parts, and never once
about **liveness** — whether any answer arrives at all. R48-2's breaker put it in one line and it is the
finding: *"A drop is the right disposal for a **losing** read, because a winner is coming behind it. It is
the wrong disposal for an **orphaned** one, and A-67 does not distinguish them."* That distinction is Part 3
below, and Parts 4–6 are it applied to the four sites where it is missing.

**Part 2 — the two defects, in the shipped code, stated once.**

- **R48-1** (`store.ts:1832`/`:1841` in `importPhotos`, `:1934`/`:1940` in `removePhoto`). Part 4's second
  half is unconditional — *"a write that changes the subject an in-flight read is reading must invalidate
  that read"* — and Part 6's table put the `supersede` *"immediately before"* the optimistic `setPhotos`,
  which is **inside** R45-4's `if (state.photos.available !== null …)`. So is the `supersede`. With
  `available === null` a byte `write` and a byte `remove` invalidate **nothing**, and Part 7 row 5 says of
  that enclosing guard, in as many words, that it *"answers a different question … a fact about the value,
  not about the ordering."* The ordering call is then nested inside it. Two measured faces: a photograph
  whose bytes are on disk reads `'missing'` after an import that raced a *Try again*; and `removePhoto` +
  `undo` reads `'ready'` over bytes that are **gone**, where §10 **A-65 T1** requires `'missing'`. It
  reproduces at `4430e34`, so it is **R47-2's fourth face** and not a regression — which is the point.
- **R48-2** (`readPhotoAvailability`'s four `return`s against `claimTransition`). A claim on
  `photoAvailability` **drops** an in-flight read, and `claimTransition()` claims that slot on **every**
  transition, including transitions that install no document and issue no replacement read. Nothing ever
  answers: `available` stays `null`, `availabilityError` stays `null`, `photosFor` reports `'loading'` for
  as long as the trip stays open. `readPhotoAvailability`'s own docstring says §10.6 property 5 is true
  *"by construction rather than by inspection"* **because every branch writes an answer**; A-67 put a
  `return` in front of all four and did not notice the docstring one screen up. This is **A-63's unresolving
  spinner**, reached by three gestures that could not reach it at `4430e34`, one of which is §2.9 **A-47**'s
  own designed banner path.

They are two halves of one question, and the proof is that **fixing either alone makes the other worse**:
hoist R48-1's `supersede` out of the value guard and it now fires exactly when `available === null`, which
is exactly when nothing will re-establish it — R48-1's fix manufactures R48-2's defect at a new site. This
entry therefore rules them together, and a builder who lands one without the other has shipped the trade
rather than the fix.

**Part 3 — the rule, and it is the sentence A-67 is missing.**

> **A bump of a slot's sequence is a promise to replace the answer it invalidated. `claim` promises an
> answer *later* and may only be taken by an operation that writes one on **every** exit, including its
> throws. `supersede` promises an answer *now*, in the same synchronous block, with no `await` between the
> two. An operation that can bump a slot and then exit having written nothing to it is a defect, however
> correct its ordering is.**

Three consequences, and they decide every site below:

1. **Ordering and liveness are separate obligations and the same primitive discharges only the first.**
   A-67 Part 3's docstrings are about ordering; nothing in the module can enforce liveness, because
   liveness is a property of the caller's exits.
2. **A slot whose value has a *pending* representation carries the obligation; one whose values are all
   terminal does not.** `photos.available === null` with `availabilityError === null` **is**
   `phase: 'loading'` (§10.6 property 5, A-63) — a pending representation, and the one state in this store
   that a user can sit in forever. `browsing === null` is *"no pane is open"*, which is terminal and
   correct. `doc` is replaced by the claimer itself. **That is why R48-2 is an unresolving spinner on one
   slot and a lost gesture on another**, and why the rule below is stricter for `photoAvailability`.
3. **The primitive follows Part 4's own criterion applied to the *writer*, not only to the field.**
   Part 4 says a field needs a slot when an async operation installs a value into it *computed from a
   snapshot taken before an `await`*. A transition's write into `photos` and `browsing` is
   `initialState().photos` and `null` — **constants, computed at the instant of writing.** Part 4's
   criterion, applied to that write, says *no claim*. A-67 applied the criterion to
   `readPhotoAvailability`'s write and never to the transition's own write into the same slot. That
   oversight is the whole of R48-2.

**Part 4 — R48-2 ruled: a transition claims `doc` and supersedes the other two at the reseed.**

Of the three shapes R48-2 offers, **(b) narrow the claim** is chosen, and (a) and (c) are refused:

- **(a) re-issue a dropped read** needs a bound so two invalidations cannot loop, needs every throwing exit
  to run an `await` inside a `catch` before its rethrow, and would have to be added at **nine** exits (Part
  4.1) — of which the finding found three. A ruling whose correctness depends on a builder finding all nine
  is the ruling that produced this finding.
- **(c) give the drop a terminal state** — the losing read writes `'unreadable'` — is the cheapest and is
  the one that lies. §10.6 property 6 renders `'unreadable'` as a read that was attempted and failed, with
  a *Try again* that will succeed immediately, over a store that is working perfectly.
- **(b) is one line of deletion and six of addition, and it closes all nine exits at once** — including the
  six the finding did not name — because an exit that never took the claim cannot strand anything.

**4.1 — Part 6's table re-derived against the shipped code, exhaustively.** Every exit of every
`claimTransition()` holder, and whether it installs a document and issues a read. **Nine exits strand an
availability read, not three** — the finding measured three and stopped:

| # | Exit | Installs? | Issues a read? | Stranded at `4316167`? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `createTrip` / `adoptTrip` / `openTrip` / `importDoc` success | yes | yes, after the release | no |
| 2 | `closeTrip`, `deleteTrip` of the **active** trip | yes (document-less reseed) | no, and none is owed — no `doc`, no listing | no |
| 3 | `deleteTrip` of a **non**-active trip | **no** | no | **yes** — the finding's face 1 |
| 4 | `openTrip`, id not in storage (`:1432`) | **no** | no | **yes** — face 2 |
| 5 | `openTrip`, corrupt document (`:1443`) | **no** | no | **yes** — face 3, and it is A-47's banner path |
| 6 | `importDoc`, `core.fromJSON` throws on garbage (`:2097`) | **no** | no | **yes**, unnamed by the finding |
| 7 | `importDoc`, `ForeignDocumentError` (`:2107`) | **no** | no | **yes**, unnamed |
| 8 | `importDoc`, id-minting exhausted (`:2117`) | **no** | no | **yes**, unnamed |
| 9 | `createTrip`/`adoptTrip`/`importDoc`, `TRANSITION_SUPERSEDED_MESSAGE` | **no** | no | no — a **newer** transition is in flight and owns the answer |
| 10 | `openTrip`/`closeTrip` supersession `return state` | **no** | no | no — same reason |
| 11 | `adoptTrip`, `ports.storage.load` rejects | **no** | no | **yes**, unnamed |
